Story & Plot

La bola negra tells an epic, sprawling story that spans three connected timelines across 75 years of history. The triptych tale intertwines the lives of three men linked by sexuality and desire, pain, and legacy. It includes a 1932 neorealist tale of a closeted young man seeking membership at a casino, a tragic wartime romance in 1937, and a 2017 lo-fi drama about a historian investigating these events.

Comedy & Entertainment

As a drama focusing on war, history, and unfinished love stories under the grip of fascism, the film leans away from traditional comedy. Its entertainment value relies instead on its novelistic approach, historical consciousness, and poetic portrait of homosexuality. The narrative offers a deeply vulnerable and confident exploration of queer storytelling rather than conventional humorous diversions.

Performances & Direction

The film features a notable cast including Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes, and Lola Dueñas. The ensemble brings emotional truth and vulnerability to this era-spanning tale. Their grounded portrayals successfully navigate the complex, interconnected lives of men facing repression and historical hardship.

Weaknesses

Despite its ambitious and moving scope, the film can occasionally feel slightly ungainly as it balances its multiple historical eras and heavy thematic elements. The sprawling structure and dense narrative weight may test the pacing for some viewers during its extensive runtime.

Final verdict

La bola negra is a powerful, era-spanning ode to queer storytellers that successfully reclaims emotional truth from history. While its sprawling triptych structure can feel slightly ungainly, the film is well worth checking out for its ambition and poetic depth. It comes recommended for viewers looking for a moving, historically conscious drama.

Overall: 3/10.

Story & Plot

The Severson family moves to a suburban neighborhood where their next-door neighbors, the Kringles, celebrate Christmas every single day of the year. The fussy city boy Mark, his wife Julie, and their young son Bobby arrive at their new home seeking a fresh start for their relationship. However, when their son becomes increasingly attached to the unusual family, Mark and Julie begin to suspect that the Kringles are not quite what they seem.

Comedy & Entertainment

The film attempts to mix holiday cheer with bloodshed through a silly, maniacal premise about the Kringle family's 365-day enthusiasm for the winter holiday. Reviewers note that the humor is cheap and the comedy feels largely unfunny, stranding a talented cast in a frustrating holiday horror-comedy hybrid. While some viewers managed to find a few laughs in the dumb, crazy vibes of the Christmas slasher, the overall comedic and entertainment value struggles to land.

Performances & Direction

The movie features a stacked cast including Ron Livingston as the fussy Mark Severson, Rachel Bilson as his wife Julie, and Jack Jewkes as their young son Bobby, alongside supporting appearances from Rob Riggle, Arden Myrin, and Thomas Lennon. Unfortunately, critics describe the experience as filled with bad acting that wastes the talented comedy cast. Despite their best efforts with the material, the actors are dragged down by a miserable execution.

Strengths

  • A stacked comedic cast
  • A fun, high-concept holiday horror premise
  • Occasional moments of entertainment in the second half

Weaknesses

The film suffers from haphazard plotting, horrible lighting, and uninspired action that comes too late to matter. Reviewers call it a ghastly mess and one of the worst movies of the year, pointing out that its cheap horror-comedy blend is terribly directed and ultimately a miserable experience.

Final verdict

Christmas at the Kringles strands a talented cast in a cheap and unfunny holiday horror-comedy that fails to live up to its fun premise. With bad acting, uninspired action, and haphazard plotting, this is a yuletide gift best left unopened. Viewers are better off holding out for a better holiday horror favorite instead.
